author: Mark Atwood
text:
Fixed, plus two defects of the same class found while in there.

1. The reported one: hour/min/sec were checked for being digits, not for being times, so '2024-03-04T99:99:99Z' parsed and came back about four days after the date it encoded. Now hour <= 23, min <= 59, sec <= 60 -- 60 allowed, since RFC 3339 5.6 reserves it for a leap second. It rolls into the next minute, which is what treating every UTC day as 86400 seconds costs, and the test pins that behaviour rather than leaving it to be discovered.

2. Separators were never checked. Only bytes[10] != 'T' was. So '2024:03:04T19:00:00Z' parsed happily: every digit pair sits where it belongs and nothing downstream notices the date separators are wrong. Now bytes 4, 7, 13 and 16 are checked.

3. days_from_civil bounded day to 1..=31 for every month, so 2024-02-31 was accepted and became 2024-03-02 -- the day count is arithmetic and never consulted a calendar. Now the real length of that month, leap years included.

All three are the same shape as the report: the parser accepted input the grammar forbids and silently reinterpreted it. For a timestamp that feeds a log's usable window, and so decides whether an SCT falls inside it, being quietly wrong is worse than being refused.

Twelve rejection cases and a matching set of acceptance cases, so the checks cannot have been made by refusing everything. Each of the three checks mutation-verified independently.
